Project No . 58000 , Rulemaking to Update Wholesale and IOU Retail
Transmission Cost Recovery in the ERCOT Region

Cyrus Reed, Legislative and Conservation Director, Sierra Club Lone Star Chapter,
cyrus.reed@sierraclub.org , 512-888-9411

August 9th, 2026


Comments of the Sierra Club on PUC Docket 58000
Sierra Club is generally supportive of the PUCT staff proposal

Summary
We support basic methodology and minimum demand charge
The Sierra Club supported SB 6, in no small part because it was specifically designed to assure
that the costs of new large loads would not be borne by other customers. PUC Docket 58000 is
a market improvement over previous versions of the rule since it specifically covers not only
transmission allocation, but would implement a minimum demand charge for all NEW large
loads and require interconnection fees paid under §25.194 relating to Large Load
Interconnection Standards and financial security forfeited under §25.194 to be used to offset
the TSP's revenue requirement. While the Sierra Club believes there may be some legal issues
with some of the proposal - since it would put requirements on certain NOIEs at the distribution
level that might exceed PUCT authority - we certainly support the intent of the rule. If it is
determined, however, that PUCT lacks authority to require NOIEs to impose certain minimum
standards, then we would suggest indicating to the legislature this may be an area where the
legislature will need to provide guidance or change.

In terms of the proposed change in transmission cost allocation - from a 15-minute 4 CP to a
30-minute 12 CP - we are in support since it would make it less likely that costs will be borne
primarily by residential customers, but still preserve some incentive still for some demand
response. That said, we believe the PUCT could still consider a methodology that would also
factor in overall energy use. As we have stated in previous comments on Project 58484, the
Commission could consider a hybrid energy, peak demand approach that would allocate 25% of
the transmission cost on energy use and 75% on a 30-minute 12 CP. The Sierra Club believes



                                                                                                   1
 this could be a slightly more fair approach since it would balance both energy use and peak
demand use on the transmission system.



Finally, while we support the minimum demand charge, we do believe there could be some
tweaks. First, we would support applying the minimum demand charge to all large loads with
over 25 MWs of demand, whether NCP or CP. Second, to give some flexibility we would suggest
that there be a percentage of the NCP applied to encourage some use of demand response and
that the 20-year fixed charge be ratcheted down over time. We are suggesting a factor between
80 to 90 percent of NCP and a fixed charge of 15 years, with a ratchet down in the final five
years.



Answers to specific questions


    1.​ Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be
different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different non-
coincident (NCP) demands?

In some cases yes. The minimum large load billing demand should be for the most part based
on the contracted amount since transmission is being built in part on this expected demand, but
in other cases the actual NCP demand on the system is more reasonable. In either case, the
minimum large load billing demand should be applied to all large loads that have a minimum of
25 MWs on the system that are required to meet interconnection standards under 25.194. In
some cases the contracted amount could be much higher than what is actually used and
allowing some flexibility could incentivize more demand response (less demand) on the system.
One potential solution would be to apply whichever is highest - ie the contracted demand for
some period, and then allow a minimum billing demand based instead on actual NCP once that
time period has passed.

2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;
b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
c. extended to a longer time period?

We would support the large load minimum billing demand be fixed for the first 10 years which
would assure some level of payment for the transmission system, and then allow some
flexibility to reduce the minimum billing for years 11-15 and 16-20 if certain conditions were
met. One approach would be to set the minimum billing at 100% in years 1-10, 90% in years
11-15 and 80% in years 16-20. This could be especially helpful where a contracted peak demand
never materializes.



                                                                                                2
 3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large load
minimum billing demand:
a. reflect a "ratcheted" demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand is
some percentage of the customer' s contracted peak demand or maximum NCP
demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline in phases
over the years, and how?
b. be based on a "weighted average" minimum billing demand, wherein the large load
minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load customer' s
contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous year and the
large load customer' s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage weighting
towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases over the years,
and how?

Again, some ratcheting of the demand makes sense as the large load continues to operate. The
Sierra Club is comfortable with any approach that assures that large loads are paying their fair
share but also rewards large loads that agree to be controllable large resources that can be
flexible to reduce demand. We would not support approaches however that would go below 80%
of the NCP.



4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as an entity
that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards)
and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power electronic based load,
specifically computational load, such as data centers and cryptocurrency mining
facilities? Responses to this question should include applicable legal support or limitations
regarding separate rate treatment for large computational loads.

SB 6 was approved in no small part because of the real challenge facing ERCOT from large
computational loads, and the latest ERCOT projections show that up to 90% of future demand
from large loads is coming from data centers. However, the statutes put into law by SB 6 did not
create a specific definition of large computational loads, nor did they authorize different
treatment of large loads. Instead, the new law applied to any NEW large load that had the
capacity to use at least 75 MWs of maximum demand, or a lower threshold as determined by
the PUCT. Therefore, we do not think it is possible to determine that separate rate treatment can
be applied only to those whose demand is based on at least 50% or greater from power
electronic based load that also are subject to §25.194 of this title (which is still in rulemaking).
However, if the PUCT wanted to apply slightly different standards to different large loads it could
instead base that rate treatment on issues like the ability to be a controllable load resource, or
ramp rate or other measures. We just do not believe that SB 6 can be interpreted to require
different standards based on the percentage of demand from electronic based load. In addition,
as stated throughout, we believe the PUCT could and should consider requiring a minimum


                                                                                                   3
 demand charge to all large loads with a maximum demand of at least 25 MWs, which would be
more protective of residential customers.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the
transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

In some limited cases, yes. In other words, in most cases, transmission upgrades resulting from
a batch study are likely to be of benefit to many customers and the wider system as opposed to
an individual load. However, if there is a facility clearly and solely required by a specific
customer' s own interconnection request that results from the batch study, then yes that facility
should be included in the definition of a transmission interconnection cost.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether the
large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these
loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission
planning studies?

There is a difference between reserving capacity for business decisionmaking and how this load
is reflected in resource adequacy reports. Assuming that a load will be fully energized and
operating in transmission planning studies and resource adequacy reports could lead to making
decisions that would be costly for other customers.

Details of the proposal and proposed changes


The Sierra Club is pleased that the PUCT staff is recommending a change in the transmission
cost allocation method and a minimum demand billing for any customer subject to large load
interconnection standards (25.194).

While we support the change from a 15-minute 4 CP method to a 30-minute 12 CP methodology,
we suggest that the PUCT should create an energy use and 12 CP methodology where energy
use is allocated for 25% of the transmission cost, and the 30-minute 12 CP is allocated the other
75%. This would assure a more fair allocation cost for transmission and reflect that
transmission infrastructure is used not just for peak use, but all year long. Still, we are generally
pleased with the change in transmission cost allocation and recognize it is an improvement.

In addition, we fully support the new minimum demand charge, where all large loads subject to
25.194 would be required to pay both a minimum demand charge and any transmission
interconnection cost. The minimum demand charge would be based either on 12 CP, NCP or
contracted peak demand - whichever is highest. While we support this approach, we do believe
there could be some flexibility after a period, since sometimes the contracted peak does not
materialize and flexibility - say after 10 years - could then encourage large loads to curtail or be
flexible with their demand going forward.




                                                                                                       4
 We wanted to also state that while we recognize the simplicity of the proposed role to assure
that large loads that must comply with Section 25.194 would be treated equally wherever they
are located within ERCOT, traditionally ERCOT and the PUCT has had less regulatory power over
non-IOU DSPs, such as those run by Municipally-Owned Utilities and electric cooperatives. The
Rule does require reporting and similar treatment of large loads in non-IOU and IOU DSPs. The
PUCT should seek input on whether its approach is statutorily allowed to avoid any legal issues
down the line. If it is not possible, we would support some language in the rule making the
provisions related to non-IOU DSPs more of a voluntary nature or suggestion. The issue of
whether the PUCT can establish minimum DSP tariff treatment of large loads in non-IOU DSPs
could be an issue for the legislature to resolve.




                                                                                              5
 Executive Summary: Comments of the Sierra Club


The Sierra Club is largely supportive of the proposed rulemaking in Project 58000.

We support the change from 15-minute 4 CP to a 30-minute 12 CP, though we would add an
energy use allocation factor so that the transmission cost was based on energy use (25%) and
12 CP (75%). This would be even more fair to residential consumers.

We support the minimum demand charge to all large load customers subject to 25.194,
although we have stated in multiple rulemakings, we would apply these standards to all large
loads with a maximum demand of at least 25 MWs.

In terms of the minimum demand charge, we are supportive of applying it based on the higher
of contracted demand, NCP or 12 CP, but we would support some flexibility after a number of
years so that there would be an incentive to encourage more flexible and controllable load
demand. Thus, perhaps after the first 10 years of operation, the minimum demand charge could
instead be based on 80 to 90% of NCP or 12 CP.

We appreciate the proposal to require reporting and equal treatment of all large loads within
ERCOT, but are not sure whether PUCT has the ability to apply such required reporting and tariffs
in non-IOU DSPs. IF it does not, the rule could be rewritten to be a suggestion to non-IOU DSPs.
